About this citation

A short summary letter of Epicurean ethics, preserved in Diogenes Laertius. Its arguments about death — that nothing is bad about it for the person who has it — are the source of the tradition's bad reputation for pleasure-seeking, which the letter itself does not support.

### Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“Death is nothing to us: for what has been dissolved has no sensation, and what has no sensation is nothing to us.”

Ancient Greek

“τὸ φρικωδέστατον οὖν τῶν κακῶν ὁ θάνατος οὐθὲν πρὸς ἡμᾶς.”

Epicurus' letter argues that death “is nothing to us” because sensation ends with dissolution. The archive's English keeps the argument's middle step (“what has been dissolved has no sensation”).

#### Forms in circulation that differ

-   “Death is nothing to us.”
-   “Death is nothing to us; when we are, death is not; when death is, we are not.”

### Attribution notes

Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus. The shorter maxim “Death is nothing to us” is Epicurus' own opening claim; the two-clause expansion often printed beside it (“when we are, death is not…”) is a later didactic paraphrase of the same argument, not a second sentence from the letter.

#### About Epicurus

Epicurus (341–270 BCE) founded the Garden school in Athens, teaching atomist physics and a therapy of desire aimed at ataraxia. He admitted women and slaves as students and wrote extensively; most works are lost, leaving letters and maxims plus Lucretius’s later poem.

### Interpretation

Epicurus is arguing that the fear of death is a mistake about what death is, not a failure of courage. His reasoning is that harm requires a subject who can experience it: once the organism has dissolved there is no one left for death to happen to. So the terror people feel is about anticipation, not about death itself. The point is therapeutic — he wants to remove a fear that he thinks ruins a life without any corresponding benefit.

#### Why it matters

The argument is more limited than it sounds: it addresses fear of being dead, not fear of dying, and not the grief of those left behind. Used precisely, it removes one specific dread and leaves the others intact.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “Death is nothing to us: for what has…”?

“Death is nothing to us: for what has…” comes from Letter to Menoeceus (c. 300 BCE), attributed to Epicurus.

#### What does Epicurus mean by death?

Some argue that death is nothing to us; others that mortality intensifies value; still others that grief and remembrance are ethical tasks. The theme sits between metaphysics and consolation. This passage enters that discussion through death, wisdom.

#### Is the wording of this Epicurus quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “Death is nothing to us: for what has been dissolved has no sensation, and what has no sensation is nothing to us.” Forms in circulation that differ: Death is nothing to us. / Death is nothing to us; when we are, death is not; when death is, we are not. The Ancient Greek reads “τὸ φρικωδέστατον οὖν τῶν κακῶν ὁ θάνατος οὐθὲν πρὸς ἡμᾶς.”

#### Is this quotation attributed correctly?

Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus. The shorter maxim “Death is nothing to us” is Epicurus' own opening claim; the two-clause expansion often printed beside it (“when we are, death is not…”) is a later didactic paraphrase of the same argument, not a second sentence from the letter.
